analysis.title: Global Equities: A US Rotation Story Becomes A Correlation Story
key_insights: UBS sales desk (Zain Nizami) says the market is moving from a rotation story to a correlation story. Index-level moves are now appearing on top of the sector rotations already underway, and the S&P 500 fell 4.36% on Nov 5 to 7,353 with 376 decliners vs 127 advancers.

The sell-off started in semiconductors and has spread. Caterpillar is the most oversold S&P 500 stock (RSI 19.5). ServiceNow is down 35% and Datadog 32% over two weeks, close behind Marvell at -40% and Intel at -39%. 26 S&P 500 constituents are down more than 20% and 72 are down more than 10% over two weeks. The median S&P 500 stock is still up 0.94% over two weeks.

The desk does not see the buyers that absorbed July's deleveraging. In July, CTAs, Retail and long-only accounts that had missed the first leg of the AI rally bought the weakness. Long-only accounts have not reacted to the price moves, and most of the desk's long-only axes are tickets from earlier in the week. Hedge fund activity is much higher than long-only.
Leverage is cleaner than in July, but the desk says cleaner positioning does not by itself create a buyer.

Semiconductors are falling at COVID speed, led by the US. The SOX is well below its 200-day moving average. The Nasdaq 100 is down 14.7% over 22 trading days, more than its full 10.9% July drawdown in roughly half the time. Intel, AMD and Nvidia have fallen further than in July, while ASML, Infineon and STMicro remain inside their July lows.

Volume does not look like capitulation. Nvidia trades 9% below its July volume, Micron 38% below and Samsung 50% below. Intel is the exception at 45% above July volume with the largest drawdown in the basket. The desk reads this as persistent distribution rather than forced liquidation, and wants Nvidia, Micron or ASML volume at or above July levels before calling a clearing.

Rising correlation is the main risk. Semis vs software and semis vs hyperscalers inverse relationships are called approaching irrational territory. Apparently non-directional hedges may lose their hedging value when gross exposure has to come down. AAPL, used as an 'anti AI' trade, has dislocated through outperformance vs the NDX. Today's best-performing hedges could become tomorrow's funding sources.

The move is predominantly US. Over two weeks the S&P 500 is down 4.0% while HSCEI is up 8.8%, Hang Seng up 8.2%, CSI 300 up 2.0% and Euro Stoxx 50 up 2.5%. The desk frames this as a question of the premium paid for US exceptionalism after this week's political developments, and as a rotation away from extreme US geographic positioning and the US multiple premium.
The desk says the 'Trump put' is more of a tailwind for rest-of-world through potentially lower oil than for broader Tech, which led recent US outperformance.

Cross-asset hedges have weakened. The S&P 500/10-year correlation moved from -0.34 in July to +0.23. Brent is near $100 and is a macro headwind. If geopolitical risk and oil ease, Europe, Asia, cyclicals and the consumer benefit. If oil rises again, cross-asset pressure intensifies.

Client feedback: the initial post-midterms response was that this was a clearing event, not a change of regime. Clients have cash but are slow to deploy it. Hedge funds are more willing to add risk, long-only managers are on the sidelines, and the dominant behaviour is rotation rather than re-grossing. Clients cite oil and the geopolitical risk premium as bigger catalysts than US political headlines.

Client views on AI are divided. Some see data-centre exposure as increasingly fragile, others argue constraints on new supply support the economics of existing capacity. Clients like defence and aerospace, European banks and Asian tech, and are more sceptical of the renewables rally.

Trade stance: the desk would start buying some semis and sell the recent 'hedging' beneficiaries against it, nibble in semis vs defensive tech, and lean against extreme relative moves (semis vs software, US vs European semis, defensives vs cyclicals, extreme geographic spreads). It separates this from calling an index bottom, especially in the US.

The desk expects squeezes but no immediate re-grossing, and says negative headlines will carry more weight and last longer in a fragile market, with negative tech headlines asymmetric. HSTECH is still down more than 20% YTD despite its bounce.

Watch list: who steps in to buy (above all, whether long-only accounts respond), the VIX, Nvidia, Micron and ASML volume vs July, the SOX vs its 200-day moving average, Brent, and the S&P 500/10-year correlation.

market_movers.rationale: The desk would start buying some semis against selling recent hedging beneficiaries. Nvidia is trading 9% below its July volume and has fallen further than in July. Nvidia volume reaching July levels is a signal the basket has cleared.
Memory fell 16% on Nov 5 but is still up 78% on the year. Micron volume is 38% below July, which the desk reads as distribution rather than capitulation.
Intel is down 39% over two weeks, the largest drawdown in the basket, on volume 45% above July.
ServiceNow is down 35% over two weeks as cloud and SaaS are hit almost as hard as semis. The desk says software and hyperscalers can become funding sources as correlations rise.
Datadog is down 32% over two weeks as SaaS sells off alongside semis.
Marvell is down 40% over two weeks, the steepest fall of the names cited.
Caterpillar is the most oversold S&P 500 stock with an RSI of 19.5, which shows the sell-off reaching industrials.
AAPL has been used as an 'anti AI' trade and is outperforming the NDX to the point of dislocation. The desk warns recent winning hedges could become funding sources.

sector_views.rationale: The desk would start buying some semis and nibble vs defensive tech, but says the group is not yet cleared. Volume is below July and long-only buyers are absent.
The desk would sell the recent hedging beneficiaries against semis. They can become funding sources as correlations rise.
Defensives are crowded and can become funding sources. The desk finds defensives vs cyclicals more interesting to lean against.
Clients cite defence and aerospace as an interesting selective opportunity.
Clients cite European banks as an interesting opportunity amid the rotation away from US positioning.
Clients show considerably more scepticism about the renewables rally.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The equity/bond hedge has weakened materially. Bonds are falling with equities.
Oil is a direct macro headwind rather than a shock absorber, and the desk calls it one of the most important variables.
The desk compares the level to the period immediately before the COVID volatility spike.
Credit stress is emerging but modest compared with the dot-com and COVID episodes.

trade_ideas.rationale: Inverse correlations between semis and software or hyperscalers are approaching irrational territory, and hedges could become funding sources as correlation normalises.
trade_ideas.risk: No capitulation yet, long-only buyers are absent and negative tech headlines may carry more weight.

trade_ideas.rationale: The desk says semis are not too far from a clearing, though it wants Nvidia, Micron or ASML volume to match July first.

trade_ideas.description: Lean against extreme relative moves: semis vs software, US vs European semis, defensives vs cyclicals, extreme geographic spreads
trade_ideas.rationale: These relative dislocations are becoming more interesting, and the desk separates them from calling an index bottom.
trade_ideas.risk: Rising correlation means relative-value and hedge positions can become more painful, and the S&P 500 could fall further.

risk_factors: Rising cross-asset correlation could make rotational and non-directional hedges costly.
No long-only buyer has appeared to absorb the selling as in July.
Oil near $100 is a headwind, and a move higher would intensify cross-asset pressure.
Bonds are falling with equities, so the equity/bond hedge has weakened.
Negative tech headlines may be asymmetric and last longer in a fragile market.
Possible further index-level downside if volume does not show a flush and buyers stay away.
vol_and_positioning: The VIX is 28.2 (Nov 5), up from 14.8 on Oct 9, and the desk says it is at levels comparable with the period immediately before the COVID volatility spike.
Correlation is rising. Rotational and non-directional hedges (semis vs software, semis vs hyperscalers) can become costly, and inverse correlations are approaching irrational territory.
Long-only accounts have not reacted. Hedge fund activity is much higher than long-only. Defensives are crowded.
Volume is below July levels in most key names, which the desk reads as persistent distribution rather than capitulation. Leverage is cleaner than in July.
Bonds are falling with equities, with S&P 500/10-year correlation at +0.23 vs -0.34 in July.
geopolitical: This week's political developments (post-midterms) are described as a potentially seismic shift in the political and geopolitical landscape, affecting the relative multiple and risk premium on US vs rest-of-world markets.
The 'Trump put' is described as a tailwind for rest-of-world through potentially lower oil.
Clients emphasise oil and the geopolitical risk premium as more important catalysts than US political headlines.

tension_points.bull_case: Leverage is cleaner than in July, US semis are down further than in July (Nasdaq 100 -14.7% in 22 days, SOX well below its 200-day), and the desk would start buying some semis against selling recent hedging beneficiaries.
tension_points.bear_case: Volume is below July in Nvidia (-9%), Micron (-38%) and Samsung (-50%), which looks like persistent distribution. Long-only buyers who absorbed July's selling are not visible, and cleaner leverage does not create a buyer.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Nvidia, Micron or ASML volume reaching July levels would signal a clearing. Long-only accounts failing to respond to the drawdown keeps the bear case in place.

tension_points.bull_case: Software, hyperscalers and defensives have worked as hiding places during the rotation.
tension_points.bear_case: As correlations rise and gross exposure comes down, these hedges can become funding sources. The S&P 500/10-year correlation has moved to +0.23 from -0.34 in July.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Correlation staying low while indices stabilise would keep the rotation framing intact.
